title: Ukraine Says It Struck Russia's Savasleyka Air Base, Damaging Five Warplanes
summary: Ukraine says it hit three MiG-31 jets and two Su-34 fighter-bombers at the Savasleyka air base in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region — the fifth strike on the base since August 2024 — in a long-range attack aimed at the aircraft behind Moscow's Kinzhal missile launches.
content:
Ukrainian forces have struck a major Russian military air base deep inside Russia, damaging five warplanes used to launch missiles and bombs at Ukraine, the Ukrainian General Staff said on Wednesday.

The strike hit the Savasleyka air base in the Nizhny Novgorod region, east of Moscow, in attacks carried out on Monday 24 November and overnight into Tuesday, according to the General Staff. Three MiG-31 interceptor jets and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were damaged and knocked out of operation "for some time", the statement said. The extent of the damage and the final number of aircraft hit are still being assessed, and officials said additional aircraft may have been affected.

Savasleyka is not just any airfield. It is one of the bases from which Russia's MiG-31 jets take off carrying Kinzhal hypersonic missiles, weapons that Moscow fires at Ukrainian cities and that are among the hardest in Russia's arsenal to intercept. Every MiG-31 taken out of service, even temporarily, trims the number of aircraft available to launch those attacks. The Su-34s hit in the same strike are the workhorses of Russia's bombing campaign, used to drop guided bombs on Ukrainian front-line positions.

The claim has not been independently verified. Russia did not immediately comment on the Ukrainian statement, and by Wednesday afternoon no satellite images showing damage at the base had surfaced publicly. The Kyiv Independent, reporting on the strike, said it could not independently verify the extent of the damage. The losses were first reported on Wednesday morning by a Ukrainian Telegram channel that tracks long-range strikes, hours before the General Staff released its own figures.

What is clear is that Savasleyka has become a repeat target. According to Ukraine's Defence Ministry, this was the fifth strike on the airfield since August 2024, a sign of how central the base has become to Kyiv's campaign against the aircraft and infrastructure behind Russia's missile attacks. Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian P-18 radar station near Karavan-Solodkyi in Russian-occupied Luhansk region in the same wave of attacks, the General Staff said on Tuesday.

The strike fits a pattern that has defined much of Ukraine's war effort this year: long-range attacks aimed at crippling Moscow's ability to keep bombing Ukrainian cities, rather than only fighting on the front line. Kyiv has steadily extended the reach of its drones and missiles, hitting refineries, airfields and radar stations hundreds of kilometres inside Russia. Moscow, for its part, has continued its own nightly bombardment of Ukrainian energy infrastructure and cities, and neither side has shown any sign of easing its campaign as winter sets in.

The timing also matters for Ukraine's allies. The European Union has stepped up financial support for Kyiv, recently [disbursing a record €7.9 billion to Ukraine](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/eu-disburses-record-7-9-billion-ukraine-november-2026), even as Russia has [revived its 2021 demands on European security](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/russia-revives-2021-nato-demands-european-security-november-2026) in the background of the war. The flow of Western support has underlined Kyiv's argument that it cannot rely on interception alone — it must also hit the aircraft that launch the missiles before they take off.

That logic is what makes Savasleyka worth striking again and again. A Patriot battery can shoot down a Kinzhal only if it is in the right place at the right moment; a MiG-31 damaged on the ground cannot launch one at all. But five aircraft, however capable, are a small share of Russia's fleet, and the base has been hit before without stopping the missile campaign. The real test of this strike will be what satellite imagery shows in the coming days — and whether Russia's Kinzhal launches from Savasleyka slow down in the weeks that follow.

For now, the episode captures the war's current shape: a grinding contest in which both sides strike deep behind enemy lines, claims are made faster than they can be verified, and each side measures success not in territory taken but in the enemy's capacity to keep attacking. According to [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/ukraine-says-it-struck-major-russian-air-base-damaging-five-planes-2026-11-25/), which first reported the Ukrainian statement, the General Staff said the damage assessment was still under way.
